speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Duhamel that Bill C-339, an act to eliminate the payments of bonuses in the public sector of Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Human Resources envelope.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate though my voice does not have its normal strength. I know it will distress all members present that I will be a little more low key than usual. However, this is such an important issue my hon. friend from St. Boniface has brought before the House that I did want to have an opportunity to make a few remarks.
I do not know exactly what his intent is but in reading this proposed piece of legislation I must say I have some concerns. I know it was not his intent to suggest that members of the Public Service of Canada ought not to receive fair, adequate compensation or anything like that. What this bill proposes to do is to take away the principle of incentive in relation to performance. Some people will disagree with that of course but it certainly is my belief that people work best when they have some incentive to do so. Fair compensation for employment and reasonable, safe working conditions are very important.
The advisory group on executive compensation in the Public Service known as the Bums group was named after the current chairman, Mr. James Bums, who is deputy chairman of Power Corporation. The group expressed the opinion and strongly held view that there should be a portion of the compensation package for senior executives put at risk, to use the group's expression, so there is some incentive.
I am not suggesting for one minute that people in senior positions in the Public Service of Canada would not give 100 per cent if their salaries were 100 per cent guaranteed. However, I think the concept that people should have incentives to work hard by having a percentage of the compensation made available by way of some sort of a bonus is important.
That is obviously one with which the advisory group agrees. I might say also it is one with which Public Service executives agree. They have agreed to that basis for compensation in their own bargaining process. I am sure it is not the intent of my hon. friend opposite to interfere with the collective bargaining process.
I realize if I start talking about the sanctity of the collective bargaining process I am sure members opposite are going to remind me very quickly it was this government that interfered with that process through the imposition of the wage restraint program on the Public Service a couple of years ago. That restraint program applied not only to members of the Public Service but also to members of this House and all people paid by the government.
That action is not normal practice. Certainly it is not the normal practice of this government because this government respects that the best way for these decisions to be made is through the collective bargaining process on the basis of market demand and so forth.
I simply remind my hon. friend and others who may wish to support this legislation that there is some potential problem inherent in an arbitrary decision being taken by Parliament. Certainly that would fly in the face

April 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
of the position he and a number of his colleagues took with respect to the public sector contract that was there a year or so ago. I merely bring that to his attention.
Maybe part of the problem lies in the use of the word bonus. A bonus to me is like getting a little prize in a Cracker Jacks box. It is something extra, something one had not necessarily expected and presumably therefore is in addition to what is expected. All that is really expected inside a box of Corn Flakes or Cheerios is the cereal but a little prize might be found inside. That is a bonus because it is something extra. I suspect the root of the legislation in part may be in the use of that particular term when in fact one might prefer the term incentive.
It is important to recall the history of this particular provision. It was taken off the compensation package at the time when this process was implemented so that if there was a salary budget equal to 100 per cent a certain percentage of that was taken back. I believe it was 15 per cent. I may be wrong about my percentages but I am talking about the principle.
What has been done in effect is to not provide a bonus as an add on. The group of employees impacted by this provision is told it is guaranteed a certain amount, which is in fact lower, 85 per cent, and there is the opportunity based on performance to earn an extra amount. I think it is important to bear that in mind.
I recall when the subject of these bonuses came up in the House a year ago, there were very flamboyant speeches by some of my hon. friends about the size of those bonuses. I think that created the context in which people thought this was not an appropriate thing.
It is important for everybody to understand that these bonuses are not an add on. In fact they are a component of the salary package that is and was already there when it was brought in.
Having said that, a bonus which is paid automatically really ceases to be an incentive. It ceases to be what it was intended to be with the use of the nefarious word bonus. If there is concern about this, what would be helpful and might warrant review is some determination or clarification of the criteria by which it will or will not be paid.
It is not easy to determine or quantify progress in some Public Service jobs. These nights whether we want to or
not, when we turn on our television sets we are being treated to hockey games. It is very easy to determine whether a hockey player gets a bonus. How many goals did he get last year? How many assists did he get? How many minutes in the penalty box? How many games did the team win? However, it is much more difficult to assess a public servant. Certainly it is difficult to quantify the performance of the individual.
If one is to determine criteria and have a clear process by which decisions will be made as to whether or not people in fact qualify for an incentive, I can understand that. The point to be made is that we must have clear criteria. It must be understood that people have to earn the incentive. It is an assumption that possibly everybody is not going to automatically get it. The automatic aspect to it can also create some progress.
At the same time however, an unattainable incentive is not really an incentive at all. When a compensation system is set up that is targeted at rewarding a person's performance, then that particular criteria should be one that if a legitimate bona fide effort is made by the individual the intent is that he or she will obtain that. In other words, the intent of the process is to encourage high performance by rewarding individual employees for the work they have done.
Administered automatically, it is a very successful system. I think it can be a beneficial system, both for the public servants impacted and Canadian taxpayers. To change that system right now would create quite a disruption. I think that a kind of political mischief was played with the system in this House a year or so ago. Except when that goes on the system works well. It serves Canadians and it serves public servants.
At the same time it provides an opportunity and a recognition for the government to be aware of the fact that Canada does have a high quality of public servants. I think all members of this House will agree that although sometimes when issues get flowing back and forth, people sometimes forget that Canadians are very well served by their public servants. We have some extraordinarily capable people.
In the case of our senior people, the compensation is often not competitive with what might be earned in the private sector. But they are just like members of Parlia-

ment. We know when we take the job what the salary and the compensation will be. That is the deal and if one does not like it then do not run for office.
I conclude with those remarks. I commend my hon. friend for bringing forward his initiative. However I cannot support it and I urge fellow members of the House to turn down this proposal also.

Mr. Speaker, I have given much consideration to Bill C-339. My constituents are continually expressing concern about our national debt and deficit each year. Therefore, I am always looking for ways to reduce spending. But I also want to take into consideration the effect that any changes we make will have on the efficiency of government and also on the people affected.
I would like to remind everyone that the present situation has the salaries of federal civil servants frozen for three years. This means last year, this year and next year there will be no bonuses paid.
Bill C-339 proposes to eliminate the payment of bonuses in the public sector of Canada. It demonstrates a lack of understanding of the performance bonus system in place for senior public servants.
I would like to briefly go into the history. In 1981 when a management category was created, it was decided to allocate a portion of the senior level's compensation package to annual re-eamable performance awards-or lump sum payments-rather than having these sums permanently built into the base salary.
The advisory group on executive compensation in the Public Service, a private sector group made up of senior executives from the Canadian business community, has been providing advice and recommendations to successive governments over the past 24 years.
The advisory group first recommended and still supports the performance bonus approach to pay. The principle that a certain portion of the compensation package for executives should be put at risk, that is individual rewards determined on the basis of their contribution to the organization, is very widespread in the private sector. Performance lump sum awards were introduced for public servants by reducing the salary range maximum to compensate for lump sum performance payments.
Therefore the replacement of the base salary adjustments with bonuses represents a cost saving because the lump sums are not compounded from one year to the next. Performance lump sums do not represent an extra payment but rather an alternative, a more cost efficient and effective method of distributing the same compensation envelope. We are talking about the same compensation envelope.
I would also like to point out that the elimination of performance bonuses would mean moving to a system which provides permanent base salary adjustments equal for all regardless of their level of performance or their contribution to the organization. Not only would this be counterproductive but also unfair and most of all, my greatest concern, more costly.
I would like to add that the passage of this bill would be going against the current trend in the private sector. Many of my constituents have advocated that we go this way. This was reported by the Conference Board of Canada and other consulting firms on the increasing portion of the compensation package that is variable or performance related.
Finally, the proposed act would have the effect of reducing the flexibility of the compensation system in favour of a rigid and more costly method of compensation. The government has the responsibility to ensure that public servants' compensation is fair and equitable compared to compensation paid in other sectors of the Canadian economy while being attentive to the interest of the Canadian taxpayers.
To date, the advice of bodies such as the advisory group on executive compensation in the Public Service has been determinant in establishing the current compensation system for executives which is recognized as one of the best systems by many other countries. We should continue to rely on those with the necessary expertise to make compensation recommendations.
I would like to do a synopsis of what this means. The advisory group on executive compensation in the Public Service expressed the opinion that a certain portion of the compensation package for senior executives should be put at risk, in line with the private sector thinking. That is what a number of my constituents are asking for and have continued to ask for.

Private Members' Business
Directly linked to performance it is misleading to suggest to Canadian taxpayers that the current system is overly generous. It is not. Performance pay does not represent additional compensation. The system of performance pay is looked at in many countries as one of the best systems in the world.
Misconceptions abound about how and why these bonuses are being paid. Performance pay is not a bonus but rather one part of a total compensation scheme for Public Service executives. Five per cent of the total package for Public Service executives is normally set aside for performance pay. I said normally because for three years it has been discontinued temporarily.
Performance pay encourages high performance by rewarding individual employees. It is an effective and economical way of encouraging high performance and is a system recognized as being cost effective.
Bill C-339 would necessarily entail changes to the salary administration plan. Automatic salary increments that are permanently added to a base salary would be a major disruption to a system that has been working well.
I will conclude by saying that I do not see any immediate or prospective gain to be achieved, at this time, by passing Bill C-339.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from St. Boniface has introduced a private member's bill dealing with a pay item that has been the cause of much frustration. Lump sum payments commonly referred to as bonuses, be they bilingual bonuses, performance bonuses or what not, have been criticized for many years.
Generally, bonuses are paid in respect of performance, which sounds reasonable to me, and in respect of bilingual capabilities, which was a commendable initiative. But over the years we have come to that conclusion. That is why the hon. member for St. Boniface saw fit, and rightly so, to deal with this problem which should have been dealt with a long time ago. Should we pay bonuses to a few supposedly qualified people, Public Service managers, or look at the system as a whole instead and tell all those who are working to make it
better, especially by making it more effective and efficient, that they deserve a lump sum payment or bonus?
My colleague made a few points and I agree with him that we should have a fair and equitable system under which all Public Service employees who have helped improve efficiency should get a bonus.
Other organizations that have been overlooked in this analysis would indeed deserve the same deal. My colleague from St. Boniface pointed out to me that some organizations are missing from the list and others, such as the NRC and all other departmental agencies, should be included. In the end, no one should be excluded.
The nearly $66 million paid in bonuses is quite a lot of money. Many people are realizing that big money is spent on bonuses, and many of those who are not getting a bonus do believe they have contributed to improved efficiency. So this is becoming a source of frustration for them, and that is understandable. Over 375,000 people work for the central government throughout the public and parapublic sector in Canada. That is a lot of people. It is essential that we have a system in which the people feel they are all working together and where bonuses are not just for a few managers according to the standards.
The question of course is that these bonuses in relation to individual compensation are disproportionate; the bonuses are very high compared to the salary. So that raises questions. My colleague from St. Boniface wonders if the time has not come to refer this issue to committee where it can be thoroughly examined, because we are not just dealing with a few thousand dollars here, but tens of millions of dollars paid in bonuses. Like my colleague, I believe it is essential to discuss this problem in committee, and in good faith of course, because these are our employees and they deserve that we take a look at the rules and criteria governing the payment of bonuses. I am convinced that the situation can be improved.
Right now there is a perception that this system is not fair. If you stop and think about it, a lot of questions come to mind. Therefore it is important that in a system like ours perception match reality. Right now it does not fit reality and the perception that people have clearly demonstrates that the system is not fair.
April 26, 1993

One wonders if the system is objective. Of course, in the face of so much criticism, we are led to believe that there is certainly a flaw somewhere. It is therefore very important that in people's minds this system be objective and fair.
As the representative of a constituency located in the national capital region, on the Quebec side where a lot of civil servants reside, I have had the opportunity to hear this issue debated on numerous occasions. I do not claim to know all the elements that should be taken into consideration to solve the problem, because I noticed that there are people who can talk about this issue for hours on end. My colleague from St. Boniface tabled a motion regarding this issue and I do not think it is a partisan initiative. It is absolutely clear that only in committee, with the co-operation of all the parties in this House, will we be able to review this issue thoroughly. Several people have worked on this issue and we must examine the different criteria in order to make this system fair. I am convinced there are ways to achieve this objective.
Moreover, we must ensure that the perception, not only on the federal government's employees' part, but also among the general public, is that the system is fair and objective.
These are essentially the comments I wanted to make altough a lot more could probably be said about this issue. I simply want to mention, for the benefit of all those who get these bonuses as well as for the many who do not, that we want this system to undergo a review. I am convinced that with good faith this can be done, thereby making the system fair for all federal public and quasi-public employees.

Mr. Speaker, there is a question to be asked: Where does fairness begin and where does it end?
The two members on the government side of the House, the member for South Shore and the member for Wild Rose, both said that we must be fairer in dealing with civil servants. I can agree with that. I think we should be fairer, but does fairness begin with the 4,750 managers in the Public Service and stop there? Does it not apply at all to the more than 200,000 who are not managers, who are not affected by this bonus program
Private Members' Business
and who do not benefit from it? They get no bonuses regardless of their performance, but the managers are entitled to bonuses.
The member for South Shore in particular said that it was based strictly on merit and performance and that if it were any other way it would not be proper. I can also agree with that. However I would like to ask the member for South Shore how many of the managers did not get a bonus? How many of the people entitled to participate in this program did not get a bonus? It would be interesting to see what the figures were and also to get some idea of what the ranges were. We know that no one outside the top 4,750 received a bonus, but how many within the group did not get one?
Both members on the government side said that it was not an add-on, that there was a deduction from the pay package and this was made available to them so they could make up what they had lost. They did not deny the possibility that they might come out ahead as well. Again, I would be very interested in seeing the figures to see how much of a deduction there was in anyone's salary before this bonus system came into effect.
I would like to make a small wager with my friend from South Shore, if we could talk about this later. I will bet there was no reduction in salaries put into effect and that people had to prove by their performance before the amount of pay they had been getting for the same work in the same position could be re-established. That is another way in which the program we have now is not fair. It is just not fair to be treating people that way.
The people in managerial positions are the ones who are getting top pay now. They average much in excess of what the people in the bargaining units are getting. Yet the bonus is available only to those in the top brackets, not to those in the lower brackets.
The freeze on salaries for those in the bargaining units will be in effect according to legislation for a period of four years now. For four years they are frozen with no movement at all. Is that fair in light of the fact that it is gradually being eaten away by what is certainly a reduced increase in the cost of living but is still a gradual increase? They are steadily losing some of their salary. Over a period of four years there will be a substantial reduction.

April 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
These other people in managerial positions have an opportunity to make that up, and perhaps even a little more, with their performance bonuses. However the people below them are taking all the heat. They are the ones on the firing line, who are dealing with line-ups of people applying for unemployment insurance, who are really stressed out, who are having problems and who are getting paid the least. Many of them are women, women who are the heads of single families. They know their salaries are frozen for a period of four years. Is it fair to them?
If we are talking about being fair to 4,750 managers how could we totally leave out of the discussion the concept of fairness with respect to the more than 200,000 who are doing the work, some of which the managers may be getting credit for when their performance bonuses are calculated? I agree we should be fair, but it is not fair to do what we are doing to the people in the bargaining unit. That is to say to them that they shall do without but those who are in charge of them and who are responsible for them are going to get performance bonuses.
It is not just performance bonuses. Reclassifications are available to people. From what we have heard through problems in our ridings and in our critic areas we know that the people in the upper ranks are being reclassified into higher and higher salary positions while people who are actually on the firing line, sometimes literally, are not.
For example, I am thinking of fisheries officers who are armed in some cases because of the hazards of their occupation. They have been trying for years before this freeze ever came into effect to get reclassification in line with their training and that take into account the hazards of the job, which is hazardous to the extent that in some cases they must carry arms. They cannot get reclassification yet the people who are supervising them, the people who are in the managerial positions, do get reclassifications as well as performance bonuses. Is that fair? I submit it is not. The government's arguments about fairness are falling on deaf ears when it is talking to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 220,000 public servants.
This program, this freeze, was initiated because of the financial condition of the government of the country,
because of the amount of money that we owe, particularly internationally. It is not making much difference there but nevertheless it is supposed to make them feel they are part of the campaign to fight the deficit, and eventually to fight the debt one would hope.
Is it fair to freeze the ones at the very bottom of the pay level and say that there will be no adjustment in their pay but the government is going to reward the ones at the top for having suggested that one way of not spending so much within the department was to freeze salaries for the ones at the bottom and to give performance bonuses to the ones at the top?
People will sacrifice. They will do their share to fight the deficit. People will do without. However if they see that this program is being applied unfairly, if the people at the top are continuing to get rewards and the people at the bottom are being denied even the possibility of maintaining their status then they are not going to feel so enthusiastic about fighting the deficit, not if the weight of fighting that deficit is placed on the shoulders of the ones who have no possible way of fighting it and no possible way of maintaining their position.
I suppose one of the things that bothered a lot of them, and we get headlines for this and sometimes perhaps there should not be, was that the Governor of the Bank of Canada had his pay scale increased by something like 25 per cent at the very time at which he was taking credit for having destroyed the economy of southern Ontario and with that eventually the economy of Canada as a whole. He wrestled inflation to the ground, regardless of the cost to Canada, regardless of the increased unemployment, regardless of the fact that the Conference Board of Canada said at the time that it was the first time in history that we were in a made-in-Canada recession. Since then it has become much worse. A performance bonus perhaps, but it was certainly a reclassification to a much higher level of salary.
How can they talk about fairness when they are leaving out of the equation any concept of treating employees fairly in the face of giving managers something extra, when they are allowing certain individuals, heads of Crown corporations for example, to move upward within their ranges and then when they reach the top of the range they increase the range higher so those individuals
April 26, 1993

are able to get regular increases? When the employees see that going on they know it is not fair.
Bill C-339 is an attempt to convince people that there will again be some kind of fairness applied. I am not saying I agree with Bill C-339, after all it is imposing something. It is doing something by handing it down, by giving a reward to somebody on the basis that they have earned a reward. That is not the way of negotiation and we do believe in negotiation.
The government's program is wrong, there is no question about that. This bill might make it look a little better for the time being, but it is not the answer in the long run. The answer in the long run is to deal fairly with everyone. That means everyone, not just the ones at the top or the ones at the bottom but all public servants. That is what this legislation should be trying to accomplish.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party must be going through a period of profound reflection and rethinking its philosophy.
A few moments ago we heard the NDP member for Nanaimo-Cowichan talk about deficit reduction and expenditure control. This is a new departure for NDP members because so far spending and borrowing money has been uppermost in their minds. That is why I was astonished, to say the least, to hear the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan of the New Democratic Party talk the way he did. This is a fundamental change in policy.
To get back to Bill C-339 introduced by the hon. member for St. Boniface, I had a chance to hear the hon. member's arguments when he presented his bill before the subcommittee on private members business. I listened to his arguments very carefully, and I must say, after giving a lot of thought to the purpose of the bill, that the hon. member for St. Boniface failed to convince me it was a good bill. There are a number of reasons for this, which I will try to explain as clearly as possible for the benefit of the members of this House, who will be asked to vote on the bill either later today or later this week.
Private Members' Business
The purpose of Bill C-339 is basically and specifically to eliminate the payment of performance bonuses in the federal Public Service. First of all, I want to say that as the bill is worded, if it were approved by this House, the government would have to eliminate all bonuses now offered in the federal Public Service, including bilingualism bonuses, isolation allowances or any kind of bonus paid by the federal government to its employees for specific reasons, in addition to performance bonuses.
My hon. colleague's bill would eliminate or abolish these bonuses. There is a whole series of them. I mentioned some just now, like bilingual bonuses, the bonuses for on-the-job training or for working in remote regions of Canada and the bonuses given to those who provide special education, for example.
Of course I am not prepared to approve this bill. I cannot approve it or vote for it because had it just concerned performance and efficiency bonuses I might have given it another look, but eliminating all the other bonuses is reason enough for me not to support it.
Furthermore, the other fundamental point on which the bill causes serious problems is that it goes against agreements reached between the federal government and its employees in collective agreements and collective bargaining. Bonuses are paid which are an integral part of the collective agreements and salary agreements that the federal government has concluded with its employees. For the government, going back on these agreements would simply mean that the employer has decided not to respect that part of the collective agreements and this would be quite unacceptable.
I listened to the argument of the member for Gatineau-La Lievre who spoke of $66 million paid in bonuses. For the benefit of those listening to us today, Canadian taxpayers, I must say that this money is already in the Public Service salary budget of the managers for whom it is intended. This is not new money that the federal government has to pay. These are not additional amounts that the federal government must provide in its budgets. They are already in the payroll package.
When the bonus system was implement 5 per cent of the Public Service payroll of those for whom these

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
bonuses were meant, the managers who met the program criteria, was set aside to pay the bonuses. This is not new or extra money.
I have thus submitted three reasons for which I must vote against the bill presented by my colleague from St. Boniface. I hope that the other members of this House will recognize that it is important for the federal government to reward its managers who do their jobs well, who look for ways to reduce spending and cut needless expenditures in the Public Service. I therefore trust that hon. members, when they recognize how effective Public Service managers are, will vote against the bill of my colleague from St. Boniface.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to take a few moments to speak on Bill C-339 this morning.
There is a perception in the public mind's eye that we are talking today about something that has become part of a system that somehow or another is abusive.
It behoves all of us to speak in defence of senior public servants who have been the recipients of performance pay since 1981, if indeed their performance warranted, to clear up the notion that what we are talking about is not just another Christmas bonus a government has decided to reward its senior managers with.
We have a system whereby senior executives are rewarded much the same as they would be if they were involved in the private sector. It is important that we have the opportunity to attract people who are competent and capable of performing jobs which are vital to the country. We need those who are as interested in becoming public servants as they would be interested in the private sector.
I have hardly begun and my time is already up. I am sorry that I do not have more time to deal with this very important topic, but suffice to say in closing we are fortunate indeed to have senior public servants in place who are professional at their jobs. It is the compensation package in place that in part attracts them to the jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Before we proceed with the debate on Motions Nos. 1 through 7,1 have read and listened very carefully to Your Honour's decision on the grouping of amendments at report stage.



April 26, 1993

I do accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker, however I must express my disappointment. I was wondering whether the Chair could assist in satisfying my concerns by indicating to me whether the Chair and the Thble took into consideration that the intent of this particular bill, Bill C-109, in part is to protect cellular privacy, to protect people from the snooping and eavesdropping that occurs out there.
I would like an explanation, if you would not mind, on how Motion No. 4 which deals with the use of scanners was acceptable whereas Motions Nos. 5 and 6 which you have ruled out of order deal with the availability of scanners. In my view they both address scanners and their availability. The one talks about preventing the import, distribution and sale as has been done in the United States in order to control access to the information that is being exchanged on a cellular telephone.
I wonder if the Chair could assist me and perhaps might even reconsider the debate around Motion No. 5.

I understand the hon. member's disappointment, but I want to reassure her that before making its decision, the Chair followed the rules and tradition in this kind of situation, where the Speaker seeks to group together motions that have the same theme.
On this point, without wanting to get into a discussion with the hon. member, I am not a procedural expert but I know that in their recommendations, the Table carefully considered the scope and substance of the amendments submitted by the hon. member. I wish to reassure her that the decision was made in accordance with the tradition and rules of this Elouse.

Mr. Speaker, I had a similar question to that of my hon. colleague because we are going to be discussing the purchasing and possession of scanners.
It certainly would be helpful for us if before getting into this discussion we would be able to make ourselves privy of the information that perhaps was discussed and

decided by the Clerk so that we would see the exact mindset on the particular question of scanners.

Mr. Speaker, in that same vein I too have a concern. My concern is that when we are looking at the whole question of scanners we are looking at cellular phones not being telephones, so to speak, but more or less being radios and having the phones' conversations picked up by scanners.
If we are allowed to sell scanners, manufacture scanners and import scanners it goes directly to the absolute use of the scanners. With the experience in the United States and other countries there is an inter-relationship where the whole picture has to be looked at. I too am rather confused as to how the differentiation was made and why the distinction not to allow Motions Nos. 5 and 6 was determined.

with a penalty of up to five years in prison for anyone who maliciously or for gain intercepts a radio based telecommunication or telephone conversation.
On this issue I would like to point out that we concur with the privacy commissioner who said at the legislative committee: "I favour a technical answer if one can be found". I will elaborate on "if one can be found" in a moment. He went on to say: "If limitations on the manufacture and distribution of scanning equipment were the answer I would find favour with that too".
Like the privacy commissioner, I have not been convinced by those who said that a technical approach would not work. We have to try it first and it has not been tried. Should we not try the banner scanning approach before moving on to jailing people for the interception of radio based telephone or cellular calls? I think that all of us in the House know how overcrowded the cells are in this country and how costly it is to maintain people in prison. This in a sense is a white collar kind of crime that could lead to a very serious infringement that could impact on the stock market. It could impact on the personal lives of people.
All that being said, where there is the potential for constraining this kind of action rather than moving immediately into the Criminal Code and into the criminal system, I think one has to look at other avenues and at the civil remedies already in the Radio Act.
I believe we should think of this as a balanced approach. It makes sense before one moves hastily into the Criminal Code, heavy sanctions, heavy fines and the long term that we have to get to that point perhaps down the road. However, it should only be as a last resort, not as the first resort, as this government moves for the first time to take a look at what is happening with the potential for scanning conversations on private cellular telephones.
I would like to point out that the cellular telephone is given a certain band width. That band width is allocated by the Department of Communications. The companies that manufacture and sell cellular telephones are using a precious public airwave. They have a certain obligation and responsibility if they are going to sell this piece of equipment without the proper kind of protection. We know that one can encrypt these phones. We also know
that with the speedy changes taking place in technology today we are digitizing phone calls and with the digitalization there is a much easier way of encoding or encrypting, whichever word you care to use, the message and the voice that are going across that air space.
There are hubs. There are distribution and radio centres on the wires across this land that transmit one's voice. One can encrypt it for the use, let us say, of the ministers, deputy ministers, army or police of this land. Then why does one not consider it equally important to stop the snooping and the eavesdropping which can be very damaging? One has just to hark back to Madam Wilhelmy and the impact on Mr. Bourassa, his credibility, and the whole argument around the constitutional accord.
I am saying there is the need for the government to find the kind of technological answers because the technology is there today. It must therefore take responsibility when it issues licences for cellular telephones to ensure that there is encrypting or protection on those lines in accordance with what the FCC is doing. The FCC has rules requiring that scanner receivers be incapable of tuning, or readily being altered to tune, within the bands allocated to the domestic public cellular radio telecommunications services.
The United States has rules and regulations and laws in this regard that will prevent and prohibit frequency converters being used in conjunction with scanners that receive or can easily be modified to receive cellular transmissions and require that scanners be incapable of converting digital cellular transmissions to voice audio. It therefore seems to me that Canada, which is in the forefront and on the leading edge of the technology and technological research certainly in the field of telecommunications, we can insist on this as a first step before we put people behind bars and we give them with incredibly high fines.
As I said, we are not encouraging the interception of cellular calls. We have a great deal of difficulty with creating an offence that could see these jails stuffed. Right now we have not moved to this control. Although the Department of Communications' functionaries tended to use an argument that there are 900,000 scanners out there, we know how ill-founded and peculiarly conceived those figures were.
April 26, 1993

In fact, when the department officials appeared before us we discovered that the figures they used included technology on the microwave, the oven in the home and the electronic door. They are talking about umpteen other things. It is not necessarily the scanners that you can go to Radio Shack to buy. However, one cannot, unless one deliberately manipulates it, have access to the band width which has the cellular telephone on it.
While we support the ban on scanners we want it to be a real act. We want this to have the kind of teeth that the minister said it would have to control snooping and eavesdropping.
I know at the heart of this matter is the whole question of the delicate balancing act between the right of individuals to privacy versus the legitimate needs of government or business to gather information. That is all very well and good. However, when I use a telephone, the fact that this is a radio phone has not been taken into consideration. This has been sold to the population as a telephone. Telephones over the twin copper wires that we are used to around this country have always protected my right to privacy and my conversation. The fact is that when I buy a cellular telephone it is not a normal telephone. I love this signal that they use to indicate a telephone, but it is really a radio. People are using the broadcasting airwaves.
There must be a way in which cellular telephone vendors make sure that one signs a document of consent so that one is made aware of the fact that one is buying a radio and not a telephone. One must be aware of the fact that one can buy encryption. Conversely, we may insist through the Department of Communications that they protect that telephone part of the spectrum. It is not then an acceptable first step to throw people into prison and to charge them under the Criminal Code when already they can be charged under the civil code through the Radiocommunication Act.
The other part of the amendment that I am bringing forward is a consequential amendment to the first one with respect to removing the Criminal Code. The third amendment that one sees in here relates to the fact that no person shall use any electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device receiving transmissions in the frequencies allocated to radio-based telephone commu-
Govemment Orders
nications that could be readily altered by the user to receive transmissions in such frequencies.
If we truly believe that we want to stop this kind of eavesdropping, that it can be damaging to families, to business, to industry and the stock exchange and that in every kind of way it can be mischievous if not dangerous, then I think one has to do the other things first. We do not have to move immediately into the Criminal Code. Therefore, I had recommended the other steps prior to moving in this direction.
I hope the government will listen, follow through and agree to this series of amendments and try technical solutions first. That is the reason why we have submitted the nature of the amendments that we propose to you. It is so that the use of those scanners is made inappropriate. It is not the Canadian way. We will use all mechanisms and all manners and all methods prior to going the Criminal Code route. Until we have given people the opportunity to know that they are infringing in a malicious and dangerous way, then it is not fair to apply a criminal sanction to this extent. I think we have other obligations first as legislators.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to support the amendments to Bill C-109 proposed by my colleague. I support them precisely for the same reasons she just gave.
We might call this bill the "Diane Wilhelmy Bill" or the "Bud Smith Bill", because there are now almost a million users of cellular phones in Canada and, up until now, that is before the two incidents involving Bud Smith, former solicitor general of British Columbia, and Diane Wilhelmy, a constitutional affairs assistant to Robert Bourassa, the premier of Quebec, we never had any problems with cellular phone communication. Never, Mr. Speaker. Do not forget that more than one million people are using cellular phones.
In my opinion, using the Criminal Code to jail people or fine them $25,000 for listening-sorry, not simply listening-you can listen to a private conversation, but you cannot say what you heard. That is the strange part about this bill that I call the "Diane Wilhelmy Bill". If you disclose the content of a conversation you inter-

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
cepted maliciously or for gain, you are guilty of an offence.
I consider this bill worthy of George Orwell's 1984, except it is late, since we are in 1993. Nine years later, George Orwell is among us. It is shameful that we should go against a precedent in the sense that protection is already provided by the Broadcasting Act. Here we are dealing with radio-based telephone communication not hard wire telephone communication. I am sure that none of the ministers opposite sincerely believe that their conversations on cellular phones are private and cannot be heard. They know very well that anyone could be listening.
This bill does not prevent anyone from listening to cellular phone communications but it prevents you from saying what you heard. That is strange.
Moreover, sanctions provided by the Criminal Code are so severe that, first, they would be very hard to apply and, second, they would allow prosecution of a person who, as a result of poor judgment, relates to his brother-in-law, his mother or a friend the content of a conversation he heard by mistake on a cellular. Do we really want that kind of Canada?
Had I heard hundreds of complaints in committee from Canadians saying: "Listen, here are the problems I have had. They have used my credit card number. They have plotted illegal or immoral activities," but there was no evidence to that effect, except for a former minister in British Columbia who made a date with his mistress. This was published in the papers and he had to deal with his wife and face his constituency. It was very embarrassing for him.
Here is what I think about what Diane Wilhelmy disclosed concerning the Charlottetown accord negotiations on constitutional issues.
I am glad to know what Ms. Wilhelmy said. I do not feel any of it was a state secret. I do not see anything wrong with the Montreal radio station CJMS or CJRP in Quebec broadcasting the information disclosed by Ms. Wilhelmy. I do not believe such action should be punished by sending a CJRP reporter to jail for a year or making him pay a $25,000 fine. That is ridiculous. It is not right.
We must ask ourselves this: Do we want to limit the interception of calls made on cellular phones? The New Democratic Party, my party, and I say yes. We believe that people should be entitled to privileged, private conversations. But is there no better way of ensuring this than by sending people to jail for a year or setting $25,000 fines? I think there is. A better alternative would be to do what the Americans have been doing for quite a while in the United States. They have simply banned the manufacture and especially the sale in the U.S. of modified devices capable of intercepting cellular phone conversations.
I must tell you that in order to pick up a cellular phone conversation, most scanners or other devices to intercept such transmissions must be tuned extremely carefully if you want to hear anything. I can tell you that even with those devices it is not easy.
There is another way. Cellphone companies are offering their customers a way to code all their conversations for $15 or $20 a month. Members of the B.C. legislature would no longer have a problem making a date with their girlfriend. Those working on the constitutional issue in Quebec would no longer risk being overheard by CJMS, CKVL or CJRP. They could speak freely. There are ways to do it.
Finally there is another method which most companies are using themselves. They would encode conversations themselves and then sell the idea that your conversation is safe from interception by other users. This is coming soon. Conversations will be coded. Why would we pass a bill to fix a problem that does not really exist? I find that disturbing when we complain that this government is always getting in the way, is too big and is introducing a bill which, for one thing, is unnecessary and second, penalizes Canadians for something that is not worth it.
In conclusion, I support my colleague's amendments and hope that the government will reconsider this bill because it is ridiculous and dangerous.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to add some comments concerning this motion by the member for Mount Royal.
April 26, 1993

There is a definite contradiction here. I frankly do not like what we are doing in using the law to market a particular product. That is essentially what is happening.
As has been said by the member for Mount Royal and the member for Chambly, this is not a phone. It is a radio. Until now the airwaves have been open. They have been open for anyone to use, and we have used them for radio and television purposes.
A cellular phone is a radio, and I think that has been stated and agreed to by the Minister of Communications. We are also saying in this House, in the ruling that has been just handed down by Your Honour, that we should not really restrict the importation of scanners. What we are really doing with this bill is allowing scanners that can pick up cellular phone conversations. That activity is all right. It is not all right in the United States but it is all right in Canada.
In Motion No. 1 we are talking about the amendments to section 184.5(1) of the Criminal Code. It says:
Every person who intercepts, by means of an electro-magnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device, maliciously or for gain, a radio-based telephone communication, if the originator of the communication or the person intended by the originator of the communication to receive it is in Canada, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years.
In Canada a lot of people are using cellular phones. Telecommunications companies want to sell cellular phones. It seems that the idea is to make cellular phones as attractive as we possibly can. How are we going to do this? We cannot say to people that their conversations on cellular phones are going to be private because we are allowing scanners to pick up the conversations. We are not telling people that anything they say on these cellular phones is not going to be used against them, is not going to be relayed to somebody else.
What we are then going to say, to step in and protect the large communication companies and the market for cellular phones, is that if people do relay the information they hear on a cellular phone through a scanner which is perfectly legal then they are going to be guilty of an indictable offence under the Criminal Code, not just a summary offence but an indictable offence for which
Government Orders
they may spend five years in incarceration. That is incredibly severe.
Why have we done that? We have done that to try to deter people from listening in on cellular phone conversations. The fact is that people are listening on scanners all the time and it will be exceedingly difficult to prove this offence. It will be exceedingly difficult to say who told whom what. It will be exceedingly difficult even to say who listened in on the conversation. We are taking airwaves that have until now been open to the public and scanners which are perfectly legal and saying that people can use them and listen in but they cannot say what they have heard. Why?
There are two reasons. The first is to try to allow cellular phones a larger share of the marketplace. The second is to tiy to ease the fears of people by assuring them their conversations are going to be private. They are not going to be private. There is nothing here that indicates these conversations are going to be private. We are going to punish people if we can prove they have listened into a conversation and relayed the contents of that conversation to somebody else.
What we are doing is very misleading. We are trying to ease the fears of people. We are trying to make them believe that everything is going to be all right if they speak on a cellular phone. We are not saying the government has to outlaw cellular phones, but I think it is vital that we be straightforward with people. It is vital they know that if they use a cellular phone what they say is subject to interception.
There is nothing horrendous about that. People are still going to use cellular phones. They are a convenience. We have them in our cars and in our homes. The amount of usage will increase. That is a given. They are not going to disappear. They are too convenient in this modem age.
There is nothing wrong in qualifying what we say over the cellular phone. There is nothing wrong with that. If there is something vital that we want to say, something of tremendous importance that we do not want anyone else to know, then we should stop our car and go somewhere else and pick up another phone, one that is not a radio, and use it to relay that information. That is not a lot to ask. It may be somewhat of an inconvenience but the fact

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
of the matter is that there is a security issue, and thereby we would not be using the law to promote cellular phones.
The use of the law is all wrong here. It is wrong. We are using it as a marketing ploy. That is not fair to Canadians. That is not fair to those who are accused. It is not fair to make that precedent. If we want to say we are going to do what we can to safeguard phones then, as the member for Mount Royal has said, we should ban scanners, at least a certain scanner. We should be aware of the technology.
There is nothing here which forces the government, the Department of Communications, to monitor the technology of the cellular phone and the scanners so that we are doing what we can to make sure we have the best technological input possible to make the cellular phone as high a grade of technology as possible so it cannot be intercepted and to make the scanners that would be able to intercept this higher technology illegal.
There must be some protection for the people we are going to accuse and perhaps incarcerate for listening in and relaying certain information. It is wrong to use the law for that purpose, I am totally opposed to this. It is wrong for the government to have the cellular phone provisions in this bill. They should be in a separate bill. This is totally unacceptable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am willing to stand down for the moment. I see someone else would like to make some comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to follow my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys on report stage of this bill.
As I was sitting here waiting for my opportunity to speak I thought of a commercial that most of us have probably seen on television. It is a commercial with regard to how Cadbury gets the caramel into the Cara-milk bar. It is a big thing about technology. There are aliens from outer space who are trying to figure out the technology that gets the caramel into the Caramilk bar.
It appears to me that the same sort of logic has gone into this bill. Instead of figuring out the simple way the technology works the Department of Communications, led by its minister, has gone the difficult route. The difficult route is this attempt to use a cannon against a mouse. It is a perversion of the Criminal Code. It is not something that we on this side of the House can tolerate.
I doubt if there is anyone, except possibly a resident alien from Mars, who is not aware of the ability almost anybody has to intercept communications on cellular phones. They are not telephones in the real sense of the word. They are radios and the radio waves are being intercepted.
Most of us in the House have cellular phones in our cars. They are a great convenience. They are a convenience because we can pick up our cellular phones, call ahead to the next meeting and say we are going to be five minutes or ten minutes late. We can call our offices to find something out. We might call a constituent to get some information. Surely most rational human beings, with the possible exception of some members of the Royal Family, know that cellular phones are not the place for communications that we would not want to read about on the front pages of local newspapers. That should be a given.
I have had conversations with friends and colleagues. One friend said to me after one such conversation on a cellular phone: "Look, will you phone me when you get home so I can find out what we were talking about?" We are all aware of the very simple way in which these conversations can be intercepted.
My colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys is absolutely right when he says: "If you are going to ban something ban the scanners or at least the specific kind of scanner that does the most damage in this particular area". We are concerned in this party about cellular privacy, but we believe that the wrong instrument has been chosen by the government in this bill.
To use the full force of the Criminal Code as a first resort is really overkill. We believe the Criminal Code should be the last resort as a method of maintaining cellular privacy. The privacy commissioner himself said
April 26, 1993

at the legislative committee he would have preferred that technical means be found to deal with cellular privacy. We could not agree more.
The general intent of our amendments to Bill C-109 is to remove the Criminal Code offences and the Radiocommunications Act offences because we believe they are the wrong instruments for dealing with cellular privacy at this time. However we are doing something very concrete to improve cellular privacy and doing so by using strong technical means, that is the banning of scanners. We believe this is supported by much of the industry. Certainly it is also supported by no one less than the privacy commissioner himself.
If we use the full force of the Criminal Code we get into a whole series of problems which we on this side of the House believe to be untenable. It is not necessary to do it at this time. Among other things-and there are times that this happens totally by accident-I have had the experience on my own cellular phone of having crossed wires and picking up somebody else's conversation through my phone. I have had the situation with the new kind of phone that I have in my car right now that suddenly something will come blaring through the speaker on that telephone when I have not even pushed a button.
If someone picks up some information with absolutely no intent and nothing other than having the equipment in the car, what exactly are the ramifications for that person if the person should use the information in some way, shape or form? The whole sense and sensibility of using Criminal Code amendments in this particular area are nonsensical. It is just unacceptable.
The privacy commissioner was not convinced by those who said that a technical approach would not work. He thinks, and we agree, that we should try it first. That is why we are so very keen on the banning of scanners. Why should we not try the banning of scanners approach before moving on to jailing people for the interception of radio-based telephone or cellular calls? We think that this is a more balanced approach and that it makes sense before this hasty move into the Criminal Code. It may be that at some point further down the road, if we discover that the banning of scanners is insufficient, we might then have resort to the Criminal Code. It would be much simpler and much better, both as an example to set for the people of Canada and a way to enforce privacy, to do
Government Orders
it by technical means rather than the use of criminal sanctions.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, George Orwell is alive and well. He is right here somewhere in the government lobby across the way directing the debate on this bill. Perhaps he is even in the House right now. What on earth is going on with the government across the way? Why would we want to have a bill that does this?
Picture this situation. The scanner is not illegal. You can sit there in front of your scanner in your underwear drinking beer, as the minister of defence would put it. We know the special affection she has for people who drink beer in their underwear. You could listen to conversations of people. If you dare say "Wilma, come and listen to this", you have committed a crime. It is a criminal offence to have said: "Wilma, come and listen to this". Is that just a trifle Orwellian or what? You do not even have to tell the next person the content of the phone call. Revealing merely the fact that such a conversation exists to your wife is a criminal act.
Where do those people across the way come from? What kind of a mindset would lead anyone to adopt legislation like that? The hon. member for Mount Royal proposed something reasonable: remove that clause from the bill. It does not make sense. It is Orwellian.
The minister across the way knows better. Heaven forbid that he would not. Otherwise no wonder our transportation industry is in a mess, if he does not know any better than that. Why can we not instead outlaw scanners if we do not want people to have them? They can have scanners. They can listen to them but to tell someone else the content or that they did listen to the conversation is illegal. To make it worse, not only is it illegal but it is a criminal offence.
Could we imagine five years later going to the Solicitor General of Canada, begging on our knees and saying: "I want a pardon. I want a Solicitor General's pardon because I have a criminal record. I told my wife that someone was speaking on the cellular phone".
How is that? Why do we want to make people criminals? Why are we doing this? It is because someone heard Mrs. Wilhelmy on her phone. There is no other reason. We would not be talking about this bill otherwise. If that is our concern, why do we need a Criminal Code amendment? We do not, and government mem-

Government Orders
bers know it. The privacy commissioner has suggested an alternative way. People across the way will not listen to common sense.
That is the justice department. It does not know anything about communications.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know. There is a problem. If the justice department and others will not listen to common sense, I say to members of the House: Those who were elected here were not elected by the officials of the justice department. They were sent here by their electors to do what is right. No wonder the member for Niagara Falls is uncomfortable with this. He should be.
We look forward to having a recorded division on this particular vote. We want to know who is in favour of an Orwellian measure like that. We want to know if the Minister of Transport is going to spend his time putting people in jail for having told their friends that they listened to someone else's call on a cellular phone. If this government has nothing better to do than to propose measures like that, it is high time it stepped aside and let someone else provide some leadership for this country.
That section of the bill is offensive. There are other measures in the bill that are good. My colleague for Mount Royal has spoken eloquently in the past and today. But that particular provision is wrong.
I say to the minister and to all his colleagues: Get on the cellular phone and phone the Minister of Communications even at the risk of someone else listening, even at the risk of some criminal telling his wife that he heard you speak. Tell the Minister of Communications to remove that offensive provision and to listen instead to the constructive advice provided by Liberal members, in particular the hon. member for Mount Royal who has suggested a better way of doing it. Listen to the privacy commissioner who has suggested a better way of doing it.
Why is it that only the Conservatives think they have the right way of doing this and everyone else is wrong? It is a little bit of the mentality that everyone else is crazy except me that they have across the way. This time they are very wrong, hopelessly wrong. This is using a sledgehammer to kill a fly and it is very offensive to all of us. It is certainly a good case of overkill, as the member for Chambly puts it, but it does more than that.
I believe that by adopting measures like this we are cheapening the Criminal Code. The Criminal Code is a serious document. I am not one of those MPs who is learned in the law, but I have respect for that document. It identifies those beliefs that are important and those things that are to be forbidden. It is an important document. By putting nonsense like this in the Criminal Code we are cheapening the whole thing. We are making the whole Criminal Code look absurd.
Imagine being the police and enforcing this stupidity. Imagine being the police and arresting someone for doing that. At the same time that contraband is coming into this country, that narcotics are being sold, that people are being murdered we are going to interrupt that important program, set it all aside to arrest and charge someone with the criminal act of having told another person that he had previously listened to a phone call.
No, my colleagues and I want no part of it, no part of it whatsoever. I say to the minister across the way that surely he should be more reasonable. I say to the parliamentary secretary: Come on, get serious. Surely we have better things to do in this Parliament than to make criminals out of ordinary Canadians for nothing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are three motions before the House. Motion No. 3 is consequential on the first two. The first two are removing the offence of intercepting and disclosing radio-based telephone communications. Members of the opposition take exception to that. They use the very standard opposition technique of always giving a solution which is impractical, unworkable or impossible.
We have heard just about every opposition member indicate the way to go is to ban scanners, that we should look at the United States and that is the way to go. There are subsequent amendments proposed by the hon. member for Mount Royal that go to what they believe is the problem, the use of the scanners.
First of all I consider that proposal to be unworkable and I believe the example used to be incorrect. The United States has not banned scanners. The United States is proposing to ban the importation and manufacture of scanners. That is not even in effect right now and
April 26, 1993

it would have the effect of grandfathering all the existing scanners. At one point it was suggested the solution to this problem was the American solution. In my opinion, that does not get at the problem at all.
The member for Mount Royal also mentioned the problem as to how many scanners there are. You bet there is a problem as to how many scanners there are in Canada because it is very difficult to define what is a scanner and what is not. It is a fact for instance that cellular or cordless telephone conversations have been picked up on AM radios. Again it is very difficult to define the problem exactly. I have no problem and I am sure other members on this side have no problem with exploring what can be done in that particular area.
However, just to say it is the use of scanners that we are going to go after, we all know scanners have legitimate uses in some cases. Many legitimate businesses operate with the use of scanners, anything from ambulance services to delivery services. I do not think it is enough to say that if certain bands are used it will be outside the law. I see the definition proposed by the opposition as including those scanners that can be readily adapted or used. Just about any scanner can be adapted to pick up cellular telephone conversations.
The whole idea to take the American route and ban the scanners is not an option, as the Americans are finding out. They are finding difficulties with this and I do not think it is one that commends itself to this House.
What we have done is to go after the act we find objectionable. That act is the disclosing and the intercepting of radio-based telecommunications. The wording that applies to the first motion is that everyone who maliciously or for gain intercepts a radio-based communication, and the second one is those who wilfully use and disclose that communication. Members of the opposition find that infuriating and offensive.
There are many Canadians, including members on this side of the House, who find the interception of their telephone conversations to be objectionable. The hon. member for Chambly in talking about conversations recorded during the constitutional negotiations said he was very pleased to know about those conversations. Well we obviously have a difference of opinion. Cana-
Govemment Orders
dians have a reasonable expectation that what they say during a telephone conversation, even on a cellular telephone, should be kept private. As the hon. member for Mount Royal says, these conversations do impact on the lives of people. When they are disclosed or when individuals are intercepting them maliciously or for gain it is impacting on the lives of individuals. I for one happen to think that is wrong. That is why we have gone directly after what it is we want.
The hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and other opposition members may portray these people as innocent, happy-go-lucky individuals who just happen to be picking up some conversations. I do not view them in that way at all. The British Columbia example, the example during the constitutional negotiations and the example of the conversations of the Royal Family, innocent individuals did not just happen to come across those conversations. These individuals are spending time, money and effort in trying to destroy other individuals. That is the type of person we are talking about and this is what these amendments to the Criminal Code are addressing.
At one point in the debate it was said that one must realize this if one of these things is being used. How about the individual who is using a land-based telephone and gets a call from somebody who is using a cellular telephone? With the technology it is very difficult and maybe impossible to tell when it is one of those conversations. What reasonable expectation does that individual have? Obviously what we are trying to do is to fill in the gaps. We are trying to make it complete so that if a land-based telephone is used there is the same expectation of privacy whether the user is speaking to someone on a cellular telephone or not. There is that.
I suggest to members of the opposition that inasmuch as there is no workable alternative at the present time to what the government is doing and inasmuch as we are going after them, I like the wording "those individuals who maliciously or for gain intercept". These are not just beautiful individuals, good upstanding Canadians; these are not the kind of people who should be protected under the present law.

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
As I say, my sympathies are with those individuals who do have their lives impacted and those individuals who do have their conversations intercepted. It seems to me that the sympathies and the support of the House should be with those individuals and not the individuals who for profit or for gain try to intercept those private communications.

In my opinion the nays have it.
