speechtext:
Pursuant to Standing Order 76(8), a recorded division on Motion No. 1 stands deferred.
If the House is agreeable, before proceeding to consideration of Motions Nos. 4 and 7,1 would like to get back to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Mount Royal and by the hon. members for Chambly and Cape Breton-The Sydneys, regarding the fact that the Chair did not allow Motions Nos. 5 and 6.
I want to thank the members for explaining their position. However, after due consideration the Chair does not feel it is necessary to reverse its ruling for the following reasons. Motion No. 4, standing in the name of the hon. member for Mount Royal, concerns use. As you
know, clause 24 prohibits the use of a telephone communication, and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Mount Royal would extend this prohibition to the use of the device to intercept a telephone communication, which reflects the intent of the legislation before the House. However Motion No. 5, also standing in the name of the hon. member for Mount Royal, concerns the manufacture, importing, distribution, lease and sale of an electromagnetic device.
This is a concept that does not appear in the bill before us today, since the bill concerns the use of a telephone communication and not manufacturing, importing, distributing or leasing. This may be an interesting concept, and the Chair would not wish to judge the content of the amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Mount Royal, although technically, according to parliamentary procedure, this amendment goes beyond the scope of Bill C-109.
That is why I suggest the hon. member seek other remedies under the Standing Orders if she wishes to pursue Motion No. 5. However, procedurally speaking, the Chair must abide by the principle approved on second reading of this bill, in other words, use of a telephone communication.
We shall now proceed to consideration of Motions No. 4 and 7, which are grouped for the purpose of debate.

Motion No. 4.
That Bill C-109 be amended in Clause 24 by adding immediately
after line 31 at page 23 the following:
"(3) Except as prescribed, no person shall use any electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device capable of
(a)	receiving transmissions in the frequencies allocated to radiobased telephone communication; or
(b)	readily being altered by the user to receive transmissions in such frequencies."
Motion No. 7.
That Bill C-109 be amended in Clause 26 by striking out lines 18
to 29 at page 24.
She said: Mr. Speaker, thank you for your analysis and your explanation of the reasons that prevented the Chair from allowing the amendment as proposed. I also appreciate the Chair's implied conclusion that I will probably have to introduce a private member's bill if I really want
April 26, 1993

to bring about some satisfactory changes. Thank you, and, although I do so with regret, I accept your ruling.

This second group of amendments allows the use of scanners as opposed to my recommendations on their manufacture, sale or importation which have been, in a sense, disallowed. I find it ironic and illusory that we can discuss the use of scanners in this bill when we cannot discuss where they come from or prevent their use. As I think we all know, scanners are not manufactured in Canada. They are imported and therefore we cannot control access to them. We just increase the potential for their misuse by allowing a place for them in this country.
It is important for us to know that the scanners we are speaking about are not only those capable of receiving cellular frequencies. I am not saying we should ban all scanners. We are not talking about every last scanner or every hobbyist's scanner, just those within the cellular band.
My hon. colleague from Niagara Falls said the solutions I presented were impractical, impossible and unusual. Perhaps they are unusual for this government, this member and his ministry because they have not had the opportunity to stop and realize that this bill is full of illusions with no practical suggestions.
I agree with him.

I cannot imagine why. That would be amazing.
We are not talking about the hobbyist scanners. I am somewhat amused when I think about the remarks made by the member for Niagara Falls. The figures that were bandied about were one million cellular telephones, which are really cellular radios. I know the government talked about 900,000 scanners but within those 900,000 scanners are the microwaves.
I would like to point out that to my knowledge the receiver capable of reception in the cellular band is not the microwave. The moment we find the mechanism to transform the microwave to receive cellular telephone calls I will agree with the figure of 900,000 scanners. Until such time we know the figures are totally false and
Government Orders
inaccurate. They include all kinds of silly nonsense we are not referring to when it comes to the kind of serious matters we are referring to in this bill.
The government would prefer to go with the concept of malicious or for gain and forget that we are talking about those people who are going to talk about having intercepted a phone call and will say: "I heard my friend talking about her problem yesterday". It may have to do with a divorce settlement, her work or a purchase on the stock exchange. She may work for a company involved in some kind of program or project that is within the realm of secrecy. She may be interested in this whole matter and talk about it on her telephone, except it is not a telephone, it is a radio phone.
As my colleague from Cape Breton pointed out, not everyone stops to think and gets out of the car to use a pay telephone where there is safety and security and no interception. Here we have interceptions.
We are not talking about all the scanners capable of picking up calls in the cellular frequency and it does not ban every last scanner. When we refer to the use of scanners it is not intended to impede hobbyists who use them. I think my colleague talked about his dad who loves to listen to the police calls and follow what is going on in terms of safety in the streets. He has a particular interest as a retired policeman. That is perfectly legal. We can have those scanners as I understand it but we are talking about an entirely different matter.
In clause 4 I strongly recommend that we allow for the use of scanners. We talk about the disallowance of the use of scanners. Except as prescribed, no person shall use any electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device or receive transmissions in the frequencies allocated to radio-based telephone communications. Under this section I am trying to amend, scanners shall not be altered by the user to receive transmissions in such frequencies. It bans those scanners capable of receiving radio-based cellular telephone communications.
Mr. Speaker, you disallowed and explained the disallowance of Motion No. 5 and I accept your ruling. You have disallowed my Motion No. 6 on the manufacture, import, distribution, lease or offer for sale of any electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other device and you will not allow that to be considered an offence.

Government Orders
You accepted the amendment that strikes out lines 18 to 29 because clause 26 generally creates the right of civil action against those contravening section 9(1.1) of the act. I suggest that we support this section because our amendment, Motion No. 6, which I read to you, Mr. Speaker, stops the summary conviction penalty from being applied to those who intercept cellular calls. It is not possible for the proceedings of such an action to be used as part of a civil action, therefore this subsection should be removed.
I think the whole area of criminality is like using a sledge-hammer unnecessarily. We are trying to do something in the technical field because the criminal field should be considered a last resort in answering the whole question of cellular privacy which is important as this becomes more and more the tool of tomorrow.
.(1315)
The question of privacy goes beyond the scope of what we are discussing in this bill and is increasingly becoming a serious issue in our society. There is the manipulation of information from 1-900 and 1-800 phone calls. Advertisers are looking for new mediums and because advertising is so expensive they want target markets. They are moving to get more and more information.
The privacy commissioner said that people's names are manipulated three to four times or more every day. The issue we are dealing with when we talk about privacy should be done at a substantive level, not at this illusory level. This does not end the interference that is creating a serious problem in our society. I think it is very important to examine the whole aspect.
In regard to this particular bill I share the view that was expressed by my colleague from Cape Breton. This particular cellular privacy issue has been inserted into a bill that looks at the very serious responsibilities of our police forces. They are charged with the security of this country and must have certain rights under certain terms and prescriptions such as the right to have a hidden camera or body pack and to overhear and pick up conversations. All that is very important. It is a shame that this bill, which we support in the sense of the amendments to the Criminal Code, has this ridiculous, poorly conceived, illusory approach. It is quite typical of how this Conservative government answers serious issues by making pictures and illusions. It does not take a practical approach and does not answer the question.
I hope the government will see its way clear to adopting the approach I have taken which my colleagues support. The opposition and the New Democratic Party see it as a favourable move in the direction of responding to privacy.

Mr. Speaker, once again I have the honour of rising to support Motion No. 4 and others which unfortunately were not allowed by the Chair. We are hearing good common sense motions from the opposition and I think we should give them the attention they deserve.
The question of scanners is very important because Bill C-109 is putting the cart before the horse. I think we want to emphasize that those particular scanners which can capture cellular telephone conversations should be gotten rid of and made illegal but that is not what we are doing.
The obvious thing about this piece of legislation is that when we talk about radio phone privacy it is actually a contradiction of terms. The radio aspect of a phone conversation uses the radio waves on the public airways. Because radio phones or cellular phones transmit over the public airways, it is practically impossible to enforce this type of legislation. That is the first problem we have with this legislation.
It is incumbent upon the government to show a serious, urgent problem when one considers how fast this legislation has been pushed through the House to this stage. Where is the urgent, serious problem that we are faced with?
I said somewhat facetiously that we could call this the Diane Wilhelmy bill or the Bud Smith bill in reference to the Solicitor General from British Columbia, I believe, who got caught making a date on a cellular phone with someone who was certainly not his wife.
He paid a political price for that. The journalists had heard it and had printed pretty much what he had said. I am sure that everyone is aware of the Diane Wilhelmy case in Quebec. She was a woman who worked in the constitutional affairs office of Mr. Bourassa's office in Quebec. She simply said how unhappy she was.
April 26, 1993

She said that the premier had caved in. I do not think he caved in on the constitutional talks. She gave some information that I am sure the premier's office would have liked kept out of the realm of the public. It is just as here on the other side of the House when the Prime Minister of Canada wanted to keep out of public hands as long as possible the poll results during the whole Charlottetown constitutional debacle. It showed from the beginning that the Canadian public was not in favour of this Charlottetown sellout of our country.
Unfortunately, now the government is trying to protect what it considers its interests are and let the public be damned. I do not think any minister or member of Parliament in this House believes for one moment that a conversation on a cellular phone right now cannot be overheard by anybody.
We know that. All one has to do is be aware of that. If one says in private what one says in public then there is no problem. If one has two different discourses or lifestyles or stories, then one is going to be in serious trouble.
I think essentially we are looking for a piece of legislation, as far as my party is concerned, which is balanced. We can support, obviously, the aspect of Bill C-109 that deals with giving police the powers they need in order to combat crime. There is no problem with that. It is a very important part of the bill.
We also support that part of the bill that gives citizens the right to sue for damages in a civil court, of course, whenever their conversations have been intercepted and treated with malice. Perhaps they lost money or the people have earned money by intercepting these conversations. That is fine. That is not in the Criminal Code. It is in the civil code. It would be in the civil code and one could do so.
We can support that as a political party. What we cannot support are the problems that this bill would create. There are some serious problems.
First, the bill attacks what it considers an urgent situation which is not really there. There is a saying: "If something is not broken, do not fix it". There is not a hue and cry across the country coming from citizens saying: "We need this legislation".
Government Orders
I have yet to hear of anyone saying: "Our credit card was stolen" or "The stock tip I had was known by many other people because of my cellular phone transmission". We are not getting this at all.
When we asked the government to come up with some examples of where, apart from government members being embarrassed, the urgency was, we did not see it. There is no urgency, no proof and no problem.
What this does do in causing problems is the following. Let us take a look at where the government did not consider the consequences of the bill, but where it could have serious consequences.
Suppose a bank president wants to monitor some of bank employees' calls and they know they are being monitored to make sure the right information is being given.
Suppose a consumer organization wants to make sure that the counsellors in the office are giving out the right information to consumers who call with a problem.
The employees know that their phone calls are being monitored. This happens all the time in business. Phone calls are monitored to make sure that customers are being served well and that the employees know exactly what the company's policies are. What happens is that it would be a violation of the law under this piece of legislation if one listens in to that call and the person calling through a cellular phone does not know that he or she is being monitored. Only the employee knows it. I hope the parliamentary secretary is taking note of this point. This would be a violation because this party that represents small business to a certain degree and large business to a great degree has decided that it is going to have the equivalent of this blockbuster bill to treat a problem that does not exist and which is going to create a problem with business.
I ask my hon. colleague who is the parliamentary secretary, through you, Mr. Speaker, whether he has ever listened in on a conversation between one of his employees and a consumer in order to see how well that employee understands the business and is transmitting what that consumer can expect from the business? Has he? I have. Other responsible businesses do. He would send me or him to jail or another business person to jail because we wanted to give good service to customers?

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
He had better go after Bell Canada, General Motors and Ford because they monitor the telephone service of their customer accounts.
Did he not know that? It is pretty late in the game right now when he has a Criminal Code violation to send these people to jail and fine them $25,000 because they want to make the service in their business competent and efficient. That is ridiculous.
Why do we have to cause people problems? Why do we have to have big government when just one easy solution is involved? That is simple. It goes back to what my colleague from Mount Royal says in her motion about restricting the use of these scanners. We do not have to ban scanners entirely. We can just make sure that the restricted use is on only those scanners that can monitor the particular radio band that picks up cellular telephone calls.
I hope and I expect the parliamentary secretary will respond to the point I raised as to what does business do if they want to listen to their employees to see how well they represent their companies. At the same time I would appreciate the parliamentary secretary looking once again at the question of those scanners that only pick up cellular telephone conversations and not all scanners as he said before.

Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to thank the Speaker for his clarification of the earlier ruling of Motions Nos. 5 and 6. I can appreciate, as the member for Mount Royal has said, the position and the points brought forward by the Speaker. Most of all, however, I particularly appreciate the time and effort he took to bring forward the clarification.
Certainly I accept the ruling of the Speaker. I see no problem with that. I was just looking at it from a certain point of view. If we do not have scanners or if we feel that scanners are the problem, how do we not allow the scanners to become a factor? That was the point I am sure the member for Mount Royal was also making.
I also want to refer to the point made by the member for Niagara Falls. He said that the U.S. has not really banned scanners. It has prohibited the manufacture and importation of scanners. I think that is a fair clarification.
I think there is a distinction there. However, the importance of the distinction depends on the individual because of how people feel about this matter. It would be a subjective point as well.
This is the point I am concerned with. The point of view in the United States is that scanners per se are not banned but the manufacture and importation of scanners is going to be prohibited. I think it still provides quite a distinction between that country and Canada.
They are saying that inevitably in the United States there is going to be an improvement in the technology of cellular phones. Cellular phones are not going to be at the state that they are now. This technology is more or less in its infancy. Cellular phones are going to improve. One is eventually going to have to have a special frequency to intercept a cellular phone call.
One is not going to be able to pick it up in an ordinary scanner, a doctored radio or a scanner that picks up police calls or ambulance calls. One is not just going to be able to make a small adjustment there to pick up the cellular phone conversations.
One will have to buy a sophisticated piece of equipment to really intercept the cellular phone calls of the future. The Americans are looking at that. They say they may have a problem right now. However, the fact of the matter, marketing being what it is, is that the cellular phone manufacturing companies are going to want to say: "We are striving to make our product safer. We are striving to give you more security. When we give you this additional security we are going to give it to you in the form of the scanners not being available to intercept your calls".
I think that is significant because there is a carrot forcing the technology companies in the United States to advance, not to mention a stick beating them from behind in the form of reduced sales.
Here we do not have that. We do not have that stick and carrot at all. We are saying that scanners are going to remain as they are or they can be approved. It does not matter.
There will always be a way.

There may always be a way but the fact of the matter is that what we are leaving in Canada is the wherewithal for companies to make a better scanner. The better scanners will be manufactured and imported, whereas in the United States with the thrust they are taking they will not be able to put that better scanner on the market or to import that better scanner. Here we will always have that incentive to bring it in. The only

April 26, 1993

restriction is that if one passes along the information then it is against the law.
There are those who say: "Heck, now you can intercept phone calls and tap phone lines". There is a considerable difference between having a scanner that happens to pick up a cellular phone conversation and someone making the concerted and detailed effort of tapping a phone line. Certainly it can be done by police forces quite easily but it is not done by the ordinary citizen. The ordinary citizen would not do that sort of thing. It is perhaps out of fear of being electrocuted if for no other reason, but they would not do it. There is a major difference.
Perhaps the analogy about a cellular phone conversation being picked up by a scanner would be perhaps a party line where someone is called, one is speaking on the phone and someone else on the party line picks up the phone and listens in on your conversation.
I think we all know of information that has been picked up perhaps not correctly and perhaps it was immoral to listen in to people's conversations, but certainly none of these people have been brought before the law. None of these people have been charged under the Criminal Code for listening in on phone conversations. When people had party lines they knew they had to be careful what they were saying. They could not say just anything at all if they wanted their conversations to remain between the person speaking and the intended recipient of the phone call. However a party line was different in one significant way. If a person did not want to speak on the party line he or she could not go to another room and use another phone. He or she might have to go to another county and use another phone. If someone has a cellular phone in a car or home and wants to say something and have security, he or she can go into the other room and use the other phone.
If we are talking about service to the public, it was more of a crying need in the time of the party line than it is now with the cellular phone. The security is now there but the government is not trying to increase that security as the United States government is. That does not necessarily make what is going on correct even with what
Government Orders
the United States is doing. I think it recognizes the shortcomings and is trying to compensate.
This government is either ignorant of the shortcomings or does not care about compensating. I think that is wrong. It is not doing the best it can for the people of Canada. I think in that regard there is a problem with the law. I hope this is challenged in the Supreme Court of Canada because I am very interested in the determination of the ruling of the Supreme Court. I do not want to give any hypothetical situations but so many come to mind it is hard to say where it would go. I am interested in the challenges of this particular legislation and these particular provisions.
I agree with the member for Mount Royal that it is unfortunate these provisions on the cellular phone are included in this bill because there are some very good things in this bill as far as the security of the public is concerned.
I would like to deal with them without having to deal with the marketing aids for these communications companies. These technological advancements make it more convenient for the public but there is a security problem. I think the public should be made aware of this. There is a real danger of telephone conversations being picked up and this is not being addressed. We are trying to use the law to market these products and I think that is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, again we on this side of the House concur with the general suggestion of the privacy commissioner that we need to try a technical solution. My hon. colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys agrees, the hon. member for Mount Royal agrees and I agree for the second time today that the Criminal Code is not the place to go. We must go to the amendments and use technology to deal with technology.
The problem of cellular interceptions can be dealt with by banning the kinds of scanners that can intercept these transmissions. We believe it is only sensible to at least attempt to deal with this by-law in this manner before introducing the Criminal Code and the full force of such amendments. It is important to note that this particular amendment deals only with scanners capable of picking up calls in the cellular frequencies and does not ban every scanner. This is particularly intended to not impede the use of scanners by hobbyists. Obviously we do

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
not want to interfere with those people who use scanners for a hobby and do not intercept various communications with any nefarious intent.
I really cannot believe that anyone who has access to the technology of cellular phones is not fully aware of just how easily interceptable they are. I go back to a particularly unhappy experience that the Nova Scotia Liberal Party had with technology when we were electing our provincial leader.
He is going to make a heck of a leader of the opposition.

I say to the Solicitor General that we got a good leader out of it. He is going to make a very good premier come May 25 as you will all see.
I did not realize I would have an opportunity to do a free time political broadcast but I thank the Solicitor General for the opportunity.
We had what was known as "dial a Grit" in Nova Scotia. It did not work the first time but the second time they got the glitches out. Someone within the phone company bureaucracy made a phone call on a cellular phone and allegedly said what the totals were for the various candidates at that point in the election. A person intercepted that call, sold the tape to CBC and the next thing we knew it was on air. This created a certain amount of consternation in the ranks. It created a lot of consternation in a lot of ranks. But when those of us who were waiting to see if the day would ever come to an end heard that story our first response was to wonder how someone, and particularly someone who worked for the phone company could be so stupid and not realize this would happen, I go back to an adage that I learned in my convent school days: "God helps those who help themselves".
There goes the phone vote.

The Solicitor General never had any training like that at all.
We cannot protect people who do not wish to be protected. We cannot help people who are going to do stupid things. That should be some sort of basic axiom. It certainly should be an axiom of the Solicitor General.
People are going to use cellular phones and we should hope they are intelligent enough not to have the kinds of conversations they would not want to read about in the public press, particularly if they happen to be public figures. We have all seen enough horrendous examples of this interception to be aware of it.
As I said in my previous comments to the other amendments, the cellular phone is a convenience, particularly for people like us in this House. It is a convenience in communicating with our office, with the people we are dealing with as we go through a series of functions in our constituencies or here in Ottawa. It is clearly not the technology to use to have an in-depth discussion about your own private thoughts, your own private political thoughts or anything else you would not want to be made public. That is only sensible.
Consequently, to talk about using far too severe methods to regulate the privacy of cellular phones is both on the face of it and in depth a ridiculous response. The response of this government and the response of this bill should be to deal first and foremost with the technology. If, in banning scanners as our amendment calls for, we discover down the road this has not been a sufficient deterrent, then the government may want to look at Criminal Code sanctions. It is far too early, far too soon in the development of this technology to call upon the resources of the Criminal Code to deal with this matter.
As the privacy commissioner said, it would obviate the necessity of going around with a lot of people. If they could not do something in the first place because the technical means did not exist for them to do it, we would not require the criminal aspect.
It is only sensible that if the scanners are banned they cannot be used and calls cannot be intercepted. That is much simpler, much better and everybody has a chance to maintain his or her privacy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a few minutes on these particular amendments.
The over-all intent of a lot of the changes is very positive. The government is trying to put in a regulatory regime which will solve a lot of the problems that have been identified by users and people in the industry for quite a long period of time. However when the government starts talking about using the heavy hand of the law to solve every problem that comes along, people should be concerned.
To bring the Criminal Code into force to stop people from eavesdropping or stealing a person's private conversation is a problem. I am not saying it should be open to everybody and there should not be a law against it. But it bothers me that the amendments which were proposed by our party are probably not going to get the support of the members opposite.
The amendments quite clearly take the lead from the United States because the cellular radio technology is shared equally by Canada and the United States and indeed by most developed countries. In the United States they have recognized that this is a problem. They have recognized that most individuals who have cellular telephones do not think of them as radios. We have heard that time and time again in the debate on report stage today. That is exactly what it is. It is a radio. It is different from a hard-line phone where individuals can only listen in if they break the law and wire-tap or eavesdrop through electronic means.
Because of the advent of cellular technology, today almost everybody in business has a cellular telephone. Almost everybody who is a professional has a cellular telephone.
A few years ago everybody had a beeper. It is just about as inexpensive today to have a telephone as it is to have a beeper. People who used the old radio phones with the whips on the backs recognized that there was a problem. Most of them were used on construction sites and places like that and people realized that their transmissions could be picked up.
Because of the type of marketing that has been employed to sell cellular technology with its cheap price and availability, people think it is just like a hard-wired telephone. They are not as careful as they should be about their conversations.
Government Orders
Many instances of interceptions, some even dealing with the Royal Family have been reported. Some have involved ministers in British Columbia where private conversations were picked up on scanners. Once they were picked up they were related to the media and caused a great deal of embarrassment. It is almost as if the mind police are there. No matter what you say somewhere somebody may be listening.
There are a number of things we can do. Although it is probably not practicable in the short term, we should try to communicate to the hundreds of thousands of individuals who have cellular telephones in their cars, pockets, briefcases or at home that they are radios and their transmissions can be picked up. They should therefore be very careful.
It is not in the interest of those individuals who sell cellular technology to tell their potential customers to be careful. The reason people buy cellular technology is to make it easier to communicate. If they are told it is easier to communicate but everybody can hear them maybe it would not be as easy to sell the product.
The amendments put forward by my colleague for Mount Royal and seconded by my colleague for Cape Breton-The Sydneys simply say to just hold it now. Maybe we are using too big a stick at this point to solve the problem because we are dealing with stealing private conversations. We should put it in the context of theft. We are imposing on people's privacy in their private conversations. One of the things we proposed in the amendment is that instead of saying we are going to make it illegal and once it is illegal that will compel people not to do it, we will deal with the technology. What we are dealing with here are scanners, some of which are capable of picking up the band waves on which cellular phones are being used. If we want to get at the problem should we not first indicate clearly in law that the manufacture, importation, distribution and sale of those types of pieces of equipment are illegal, that one cannot do it?
It seems to me not to deal with that problem first will mean that we basically have a law on the books which is not enforceable. What are we going to have? Are we going to have the cellular police? How many people is the government going to have? Will there be a policeman in the back seat of everybody's car monitoring to see

April 26, 1993
Government Orders
if there is some static on the line or will there be somebody in everybody's basement that has a scanner in their living-room? How in the name of goodness does this bill put forward a reasonable solution to the problem?
We do not have 10 scanners or 100 scanners. There are tens of thousands of scanners out there and tens of thousands of scanners on the shelves in Radio Shack and other places that have the capability to pick up those bands on which cellular conversations take place. It seems to me that the first thing we should do is make sure that those pieces of equipment are not available in the marketplace and that we make the distribution, sale or ownership illegal.
I think if we do that, we will find that we are not putting the cart before the horse; we are putting the horse before the cart. The government for some reason has not chosen to do that.
I really do get concerned. In a political science class, I think it was at Prince Andrew High School about three years ago during the abortion debate when we were talking about the various proposals that were put forward, they asked the question is a law that is unenforceable really a law. If law makers pass laws knowing that they cannot be enforced, have the law makers not been negligent? Do we simply wash our hands, saying we have dealt with the issue knowing that the solution that has been proposed is not enforceable? I think we do a great disservice to the Canadian public when we take that type of approach. I think we do a great disservice.
I have heard no compelling evidence from anybody that the solution proposed in this bill is actually workable. I cannot figure out for the life of me how just by making the use of these things illegal and putting them under the Criminal Code and all of a sudden having some enforcement in some way will make people comply with it up front.
Indeed if we look at what they have done in the United States at the Federal Communications Commission there are pieces of legislation going forward prohibiting marketing radio scanners capable of intercepting cellular phone conversations. They have decided the way that one deals with this problem is to nip it in the bud. You make sure there is not a problem by making sure that
these types of equipment cannot be purchased, imported, sold or owned, rather than just saying: "Everybody can have it but we are just going to make it illegal".
It is like saying to everybody: "You can all have a gun, but it is illegal if you put bullets in it and we are going to have people going around to make sure you do not have bullets in your gun". It is the same type of thing. Maybe if we have a problem with bullets and guns we should deal with the guns first.
I support the amendment that has been put forward by my colleague from Mount Royal. I think she makes eminent good sense. She normally does when she speaks in this House. I dare say that there is no one in this House, probably including the minister-yes, including the minister-that is as knowledgeable in the field or has worked as hard in her official capacity as the communications critic, as does the member. She does not put things forward just to be divisive or to cause debate. She puts them forward to try to better the legislation.
I would have thought by this point in time that the members opposite would have recognized that and seen the pearls of wisdom that she does put forward on pieces of legislation like this and would have accepted it.
In conclusion, it is not just the Liberal Party that is saying that perhaps the government is putting the cart before the horse and is proposing solutions that may not work. Indeed the commissioner himself indicated very clearly at the committee hearings that he would have preferred that technical means be found to deal with cellular privacy rather than using that big blunt instrument of the Criminal Code and we in this party concur.
As a result, we agree fully with the suggestions of the privacy commissioner that we have to try to find technical solutions to this problem first before using the heavy hand of the Criminal Code and the jail system which is already under great strains to deal with what otherwise might a problem more easily arrived at by adopting the amendments to clause 24 on page 23.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do agree with the hon. member for Mount Royal on one thing. It is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to define how many scanners are in Canada.
April 26, 1993

She was quite correct when she said that the figure of
900,000	scanners was bandied about several times during the committee hearings. It seems to me that what she was saying lends itself to what the government is trying to do. Because it is impossible to just state what exactly is or is not a scanner or what is or is not capable of picking up cellular conversations, it is better to do what the government is doing. We will make it illegal if one is the kind of individual who wants to sell other people's conversations.
I think the proposal suggested by the Liberal Party is completely unworkable. The Liberals want to ban any device capable of picking up a cellular telephone conversation. UHF receivers, including tens of thousands of older televisions, are capable of picking up these conversations. Many ordinary radios are capable of picking up those conversations. Much of the sophisticated equipment used anywhere from airports to businesses is capable of or can be adapted to picking it up. That is why the so-called solution of the Liberal Party, supported by the New Democratic Party, just cannot work. It cannot work and they know it cannot work.
That is the part of the argument by the member for Mount Royal with which I completely agree. Yes, she is right, I do not know whether there are 500,000 or 900,000 or 20,000. However, we are trying to get at what we think is wrong. We are getting at the electronic eavesdroppers. I am surprised that the hon. members would find that so offensive.
They suggest that we have to keep looking for a technological solution. They say that if one does not like people overhearing one's conversation then get a better encrypter or put in a more sophisticated encrypter. I can say with respect to that we are losing the war in electronics. The electronics are always going to be ahead of us. I think we are being short-sighted. We are doing ourselves a disfavour by not supporting the amendments that we have here because privacy affects all of us.
I suggest to the hon. member for Chambly that he should not be so worried about the businesses that want to listen in on their employees' conversations. They will be able to look after their own interests, I am quite certain. It is not necessary for him to take up their cause. They will do just fine.
Government Orders
The other individuals in the Liberal Party say: "Just get a technological solution". We are losing the war to the computer. Our privacy is being threatened every day. We heard evidence on that. We have less and less protection. That is why the government says: "If you are in the business of being a peeping Tom with respect to this sort of thing, if you are a professional snoop, if you are in the business of selling other people's conversations, then you are the kind of person who we do not like". These are the kind of people who are affected by legislation such as this. I say not to buy the argument that somehow we will just stay one step ahead of the computers and the technology. We have been losing that battle for a long time.
There are people in the United States now who, contrary to the suggestion that we should be looking at what they are doing, are looking at the route that we have taken on this because they realize that this is a threat to the privacy of their citizens as well. It is one that I believe commends itself to the House.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday I raised questions in the House concerning the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and President Judy Rebick's selection of the lobby group's new president.
I raised the issue because surely there is a Canadian woman from Newfoundland to Yukon who could lead NAC. There are many Canadians who would like answers from Ms. Rebick on her exclusive manners. There are many taxpayers who would like to know where their tax money is going.
Beyond this, I find it highly insulting that Ms. Rebick would hide in the shadows of political correctness and not answer to the concern many Canadian women have: Who is representing them?
To throw labels and insults at people is not responsible. To ask about a person's work status in Canada when she is in our country only on a student visa is a legitimate question.
I maintain that Canadian women's concerns and interests are best represented by a Canadian, a citizen who has lived here and understands the issues facing our country's women.
Even more important than this, Canadian women should be given an opportunity to choose who will represent them.

Mr. Speaker, I recently spent one week in Croatia and my visits to those Canadians involved in the situation, be it through the International Red Cross, refugee camps, the civilian police, the military or the European Community monitoring mission, revealed that all are conducting themselves admirably. All Canadians should be proud and supportive.
Our Armed Forces personnel, in their own words, are well trained and well equipped and, in the words of others, they are well respected. There is imminent
April 26, 1993

danger, even death, but Canadians are prepared to do what is necessary.
They do wonder if the people back home are aware of the gravity of the situation. They wonder why there is not more debate in the House. They wonder why there has been no official political delegation to see first hand the situation. They wonder why the deluge of mail at Christmas has been followed by months of little correspondence.
Let us support these people who are performing most difficult tasks in an unspeakable environment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the minister of fisheries and the department officials in Ottawa, Moncton, Anti-gonish and Halifax for responding to the needs of the residents along the Northumberland Strait and the Five Island shore who had expressed their concerns about the future of the clam fishery on both shores.
The minister and the officials addressed the situation in a timely and appropriate manner which appears will resolve the concerns of the people involved. Under the new regulations recently announced DFO officials are now able to take the necessary action to protect the clam beds and conserve the resource for future generations.
DFO officials in Moncton, Antigonish and Halifax have taken a key interest in this issue and have met with the clam fishermen involved to hear their concerns and listen to their advice.
The quick action taken by the department has resulted in the defusing of a very controversial subject in my area and has gone a long way toward conserving the resource. I would like to thank the minister and his officials involved for their co-operation and assistance.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the matter of peacekeeping, which is of growing importance and concern to many Canadians.
We are among the best in the world when it comes to this task, with some 4,500 Canadian peacekeepers stationed around the globe. However it is dangerous and the results are often frightening. This past Saturday in the former Yugoslavia two Canadian soldiers were injured when their armoured personnel carrier hit an anti-tank mine.
Canada has never refused an invitation to join a mission. Right now we can meet our current duties but we do not have the resources to join new peacekeeping efforts. Not surprisingly, the government has no plan for Canada and its peacekeeping role. This lack of planning will result in more accidents, more wounded and sometimes more killed.
More often in the new world of peacemaking our troops have been sent in to what can only be called hot spots. More often we are asking our forces to risk their lives during these operations.
Is it too much to ask this government to make a commitment to our forces by creating a solid Canadian policy on peacekeeping? I should say not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, National Consumer Week starts today. With its theme It's Everybody's Business, it focuses on raising public awareness of issues affecting consumers and the marketplace.
The government is repeating last year's theme because it is convinced that all economic partners in this country should be consulted on measures dealing with consumer issues. All groups in our society must take an active part in these consultations.
The theme focuses on generating public interest in marketplace issues and highlights the important role consumers, educators, businesses and government play in addressing marketplace issues.
This week, all Canadians are invited to rediscover the benefits of being informed consumers and thus helping to develop a fair, efficient and competitive marketplace.

April 26, 1993
National Consumer Week will give Canadians an opportunity to become better informed on issues that concern all consumers and on their own rights and responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the government's attention to the continuing high rate of suicide among aboriginal youth. Within the last few weeks several more young people in the Northwest Territories have taken their own lives and several others have attempted suicide.
Earlier this month a special meeting was held in Iqaluit. The high school guidance counsellor is overwhelmed by the number of students who have told him they are thinking of killing themselves. In the words of the counsellor: "The numbers are staggering". Throughout Canada, from the Arctic to the east and west coasts, aboriginal youth are trying and taking their own lives at horrifying rates.
Miles Morrisseau, an aboriginal writer, talked in his column last week about how the will to live has been drained from many aboriginal youth by hopelessness and the sense that no one cares. He suggested calling off 1993 as the year of the indigenous peoples until there is something to celebrate. He said it is a tragic year when the words "succeed" and "native" are most often put together when the story is about suicide.
I do not want the government to forget amid its current preoccupations this terrible crisis in aboriginal communities. The government must now show it cares.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday the people of the municipality of La Sarre paid a last moving tribute to their mayor, Guy Carignan, who died on Ibesday, April 20.
Elected mayor of La Sarre not long ago, Guy Carignan leaves us with the memory of a man who was kind, honest, very generous with his time, trustworthy and totally dedicated to his community.
Guy Carignan was always ready to defend a just cause and the interests of his region.
To his wife and children, I wish to extend my sincere condolences and hope they will find the strength to face this ordeal. I would like to add that Guy will always be an inspiration to our community, and especially to its younger members.
To Guy Carignan, one last word: Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced his much delayed assistance package for groundfisher-men in Atlantic Canada. Unfortunately the government intends to provide income support for only one year.
Does the minister expect a crisis that was over eight years in the making to go away in just one year? Some fishermen in my riding are looking at reductions of over $100,000 because of the quota cuts. Despite this the government is providing only $406 a week in assistance. How can the minister expect fishermen to make their boat payments, pay their mortgages and still put food on the table?
Conservative fisheries mismanagement has extended itself into a half-baked plan to help fishermen. Fishermen deserve better government than they have been getting, and come this fall they will get that in a Liberal government.

Mr. Speaker, I have become aware of a situation in which nonunionized workers of the federal government are being denied their UI benefits.
During the last PSAC strike many non-unionized workers at the taxation centre in Winnipeg crossed the PSAC picket line and went to work. Shortly into the strike these workers were sent home because of equipment failure. As a result many applied for UI benefits which I believe they are entitled to receive.

These workers should not be penalized because of the position taken by their unionized co-workers. They came to work and through no fault of their own were not able to perform their duties. These people deserve UI benefits and I will continue to pursue this matter to ensure that their benefits are reinstated.

Mr. Speaker, 10 years ago when there was a Liberal federal government Canada's Catholic bishops called for alternative people-oriented economic and social policies. In particular they urged the government not to fight inflation by creating more unemployment.
This month the bishops restated their concerns and pointed out the social crisis created by widespread and sustained unemployment, including the fact that thousands of young Canadians have little hope for the future.
The bishops reminded us all that in the 1980s the Liberal government put control of inflation above job creation and "forced wage-earners and the unemployed to carry an unfair burden". Today they point out that the Conservative government is "forcing the unemployed to carry a disproportionate burden".
They conclude that "as long as job creation is not a firm priority the current social crisis will only worsen". They propose that Canada needs "new economic strategies that will create decent jobs and revitalize social programs". They stress the need for close co-operation between governments, business, labour and other groups in society in working out a new vision for Canadian society.
The similarities between the ethical approaches to the economy proposed by the Catholic bishops and the New Democrats' job strategy are striking. On this budget day I know the government will not listen to the NDP but why will it not listen to the Catholic bishops? Can it be because these church leaders have labelled their economic policies and those pursued by the Liberals as unethical?

Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear that the Nova Scotia government is prepared to follow the lead of the federal government in providing compensation to victims of contaminated blood or blood products.
However I was very disturbed to hear the Ontario health minister admit that the provinces had agreed to hold a united front to stop any such assistance to these unfortunate victims of the system, many of whom have already died, are dying or will die. I cannot believe the callousness of this action.
I was also very annoyed to hear the health minister of B.C. say that the subject needed more study. This subject has been studied to death. What is needed is some immediate compassionate action to assist these innocent people who are facing horrendous mental, physical and financial problems.
Provincial health ministers should be meeting right now to prepare a plan for such assistance before more victims are dead and their families are destroyed both emotionally and financially.

Mr. Speaker, few issues have raised such passion as the question of public signs in Quebec. Overzealous, restrictive legislation has not conveyed images of an open, respectful society. Bill 178 is repugnant. Its message makes nonfrancophones feel like second class citizens and has become an embarrassment for Quebec. Majority rights must never be obtained through the suppression of minorities.
This weekend we noted with encouragement and a sense of justice that the Quebec Liberal council proposed amendments to Bill 178 which will create greater linguistic expression. Now the government is to act. Hopefully in the forthcoming draft of the law not only free expression but the important issue of access to English language education for Canadian children without having to prove their eligibility will be addressed.

April 26, 1993
Oral Questions
The right to bilingualism for communities like Rosem-ere should also be preserved. The English language hospitals and health networks should be protected, as should the travelling public in the matter of road and resort signage.
While I support the promotion of the French language for all of us we should never have reached a time in our society when the right to express one's self inside or outside in either official language has become an issue. It is urgent to correct this unnecessary policy which ignores minority rights.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, although one of the few areas with more money in 1993, the Challenge program will not be able to fulfil the need for student summer employment nor gain the potential the student work force offers. That is why it remains important for every business and institution in Canada to stretch as much as they possibly can to help temporary employment, particularly for those students who need it to continue their education.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. I am very pleased the minister has changed her mind and has come back to Parliament, because I believe Canadians are very deeply concerned about the status and safety of our forces in Bosnia.
Contrary to what the government House leader said in answer to questions last Friday, we have heard the following kinds of statements made. The UN commander in Yugoslavia said the order is that Canadians "protect Srebrenica". The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that having declared Srebrenica as a safe haven it is important that the UN live up to its commitments. An official at external affairs said there is a line being drawn for the first time.
Canadians want to know what line is exactly being drawn. What mandate is being given to our troops? Are they being asked to defend the civilians in Srebrenica? Are they being given the proper equipment to fulfil that task? Will reinforcements be given to them? Does the government have a contingency plan to rescue these troops in case of a serious attack?
Possibly the Challenge program could also change its focus so that more funds are used on a matching basis with employers to create the greatest number of jobs. For example, if the $2.50 base rate were allocated to a larger portion of the program on the basis of matching or higher sharing by employers, the total number of students employed would likely increase.
That is not to discount institutional or non-profit employment where Challenge pays a higher share, but perhaps even those budgets could be stretched on a large sharing basis so as to create an ever larger number of student jobs. The Challenge program is a good one but will not fulfil the need alone.
Canadian employers in all sectors should strive to tap the student work potential this summer. It is a good investment in the future of our nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
General McDougall, Corporal Campbell.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-I thought the hon. member might want to hear a response from myself since I have been in very close touch not just with our own military but also with our international allies on this subject.
First of all we, as others do, recognize the risks in Srebrenica which exist also in other parts of Bosnia and in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. They are obviously doing a superb job. I think all Canadians would applaud the job they are doing there.

Hear, hear.

April 26, 1993

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had a lengthy discussion with our military this morning. They are confident in the professionalism and in the leadership of our own troops on the ground in Srebrenica as elsewhere. Obviously we recognize the extra sensitivity in Srebrenica.
As always there are contingency plans. There are UN plans for any kind of change in what happens on the ground whether that should be some kind of attack or whether there is a need for a withdrawal. Should the situation change in any way there are contingency plans that have been established by UNPROFOR of which our people on the ground have been a part.
Both the Minister of National Defence and myself are fully confident in our military and the actions they have taken in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, seeing as the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not answer the question I put, I will repeat the question for the Minister of National Defence.
No one is questioning the professionalism or the competence of our troops. We are questioning the mandate that has been given and whether in fact the troops, about 120 in number, very lightly equipped, are now being asked to protect civilians in that endangered outpost, whether the Government of Canada has agreed to that, and if that mandate is in fact in place whether we are giving them the proper equipment, ensuring they will have reinforcements and primarily ensuring the safety and protection of the troops in a very vulnerable, sensitive position.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to underline that the UN mission going on in Srebrenica is under UN command. It is worth carrying out and it is being well carried out. It is a success because the shooting has stopped in that region as a result of the Canadian presence there and as a result of the actions that have been taken by describing that as a safe haven.
If there is any change in the situation then there will be action taken. There are contingency plans to ensure that there are reinforcements available, including air cover that has been specifically and explicitly promised by our allies, and other contingency plans that will assist our people on the ground to know exactly what to do should the situation change.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, we are still not getting an answer to a very serious question.
Oh, oh.

The Tory government may laugh about this but it is not a laughing matter. It is not a laughing matter to be given the mandate to provide for the protection of our troops at the same time that they are not being given the kind of equipment or back-up they need. We want to know exactly.
The minister talks about change of conditions. We had today the imposition of a new sanctions program. Serious discussion is now being looked at in terms of air strikes. We do not know what the government's position is on that because clearly it will bring about retaliation.
Can the Minister of National Defence, the Secretary of State for External Affairs or somebody tell us exactly what is the Canadian position? Do we support these air strikes? Do we support a mandate where Canadian troops have been given the mission to defend civilians in Srebrenica?
When will we have a full and proper debate in this House so that the Parliament of Canada will find out exactly what is going on and we can have the consent of the Canadian people through their elected representatives?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the first place I think Canadian people, from everything they have been telling me, are strongly supportive of what we are doing in Yugoslavia.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That mission as well, but there is a very explicit mission for the Canadians who are in Srebrenica, that is that it is a humanitarian effort and it is the evacuation of the wounded and of other civilians who may be ill. That is what the mission is all about.
The Canadians like others are in a position of making a determination as to what is the extent of their capacity to defend the town. If the town requires defending then

April 26, 1993
Oral Questions
there will be reinforcement of the Canadians in order to defend it.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of National Defence said that the beating incident in Somalia of March 16 was not conveyed to headquarters in Ottawa and so Canadians did not find out about it. Since then we all know otherwise. We know that the minister was briefed the next day.
I want to ask the Minister of National Defence: Why was this House given misleading and inaccurate information?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that I will be making a statement on this and other events in the period allotted to ministerial statements immediately after Question Period, but the House was not given incorrect or misleading information.
With respect to the event to which the hon. member refers, I was briefed the next day that a death had taken place. It was not until March 31 that it was communicated to me that death had now been characterized as a homicide or as a murder. The press release was released, and I had it in the House the last time I was here, in Mogadishu. It is the custom of the armed forces to make those releases on the spot where the events have occurred.
I indicated that in my view there should have been better communication between Mogadishu. I am sorry, I think it was actually posted in Belet Huen. There should have been better communication between Somalia and the Department of National Defence. I have taken steps to ensure that kind of communication is now in place so that there is full understanding in Ottawa of all press releases and all information that have been made available throughout the world where our forces are in theatre.

Mr. Speaker, the point here is that Parliament has had to find out about these incidents in Somalia through the media, through private letters and through questions in the House. We know now that the minister has had the knowledge and information but she failed to disclose them. As a result unfortunately unnecessary confusion
and speculation have added to a serious and sensitive situation.
Will the Minister of National Defence undertake a full-time commitment to regularly and openly brief Parliament on the conduct of Canadian peacekeeping operations without delay as they occur?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is already the practice of the Department of National Defence to make public all the events that occur around the world. These have been well covered.
As I said, I will be making a statement in the House this afternoon, but I am not aware of any events that ought to have been disclosed to Parliament that were not disclosed to Parliament. If that hon. member has an example of something that should have been communicated I will be more than happy to take it under advisement.
We have been fully communicative of all the events that have touched on the particular activities of our peacekeeping forces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence.
In respect of the death on March 4, the early reports were that it was the death of a Somali and there was no hint of any allegation of homicide in that case until just last week.
Was the minister similarly kept in the dark by her own department, as she now says she was in respect of the March 16 incident and, if so, where did the cover-up begin and end? Was the minister herself the victim of a cover-up? Finally can the minister tell us what she did when she discovered she had not been told the full story by her own department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was no cover-up and no effort to withhold information.
I have made every effort since the beginning of these events to ensure that they are disclosed to the public, but that they are disclosed to the public in a way that does not compromise my obligations under the National Defence Act to remain scrupulously neutral as to the interpretation of those events in light of the possibility that I may have to play one of my roles under the
April 26, 1993

National Defence Act in a quasi-judicial capacity, which is why I have instructed General Reay, the Judge Advocate General and others to meet publicly to disclose all events and all facts that relate to these particular circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I take it from the minister's answer that the people in the field who appear to have kept that information from the minister are still there and are still responsible for the command of our forces there.
In February the minister was interviewed in Halifax about a proposal that Alexa McDonough and others have made about having a peacekeeping centre in Cornwallis. The minister then said, and I quote: "The idea of a peacekeeping training centre is a wonderful idea for most people who do not know anything about peacekeeping, but I have had discussions with senior members of the Canadian military who are a bit perplexed as to what you would teach people about the normal skill of a good combat-ready military".
Is the minister, in light of what we have now heard about events in Somalia, still as convinced as she was in February that she alone knows that combat readiness is all the skills that are necessary to deal with as difficult and complex a situation as our forces are in in Somalia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a broad variety of skills and preparation required in deploying our troops wherever they are in the world, whether it is on humanitarian issues, peacekeeping or peacemaking operations. This training is carried out in the course of the training of the Canadian Armed Forces. It is for that reason senior members of the Department of National Defence were perplexed as to what additional kinds of things might be provided in a separate institution that are not provided now.
It is important for us always, and I as Minister of National Defence responsible for the direction of the armed forces take the responsibility seriously, to ensure that training which is part of the normal training of the Canadian Armed Forces is in fact carried out to the highest standard.

Mr. Speaker, on May 1 a human rights organization called African Rights will be
Oral Questions
issuing a report in which it reports that our country is not the only one with these kinds of problems in Somalia, that in fact 230 Somalis have been killed by the multina-tion9zal forces who are there under Operation Restore Hope. They have also said that the Somalis have been marginalized and Operation Restore Hope has achieved little or nothing of substance.
I wonder if the minister would agree that it is appropriate in a sense of priorities that we are spending more this year on our peacekeeping operation in Somalia than the entire CIDA budget for development assistance in all of Africa.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think that anyone who has seen the reports of the work that has been done by the Canadian forces and others in Somalia would for a moment think that anything was being accomplished there other than the alleviation of human suffering in enormous quality. That is what our people have been doing and that is what they will continue to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence. This is a time of record unemployment. One million Canadian children are living in poverty and 700,000 Canadian children have used food banks. It is no time to spend close to $6 billion on the EH-101 cold war helicopters.
In the January 19, 1993 Victoria Times-Colonist the minister had this to say: "I am convinced the helicopter decision was the correct one".
I want to ask her today, in view of the overwhelming evidence to the contrary, does she still think today that that decision was a correct one and, if so, why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is a correct one because I have seen no compelling evidence to the contrary.

April 26, 1993
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that this minister and this government put cold war helicopters above unemployed Canadians and hungry children in Canada.
The minister in The Ottawa Sun on February 2 said: "I", the innocent Minister of Justice at that time, "posed the question about the helicopters but I was persuaded it was good policy and that the cost of cancelling it would be unacceptable".
Four out of five Canadians tell the minister and tell the government they do not want these helicopters bought at this time. Why are the minister and the government refusing to cancel this decision today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all with respect to the question of the unemployed, there will be 45,000 person-years of employment for Canadians as a result of this particular contract. I do not think that is insignificant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to address an issue which I know has been of concern to the Canadian people.
A series of incidents has taken place in Somalia which casts a shadow on the fine reputation of the Canadian forces. In the search for truth, for justice and to reassure the men and women of the Canadian forces and their families, these incidents must be addressed.
Four incidents are of particular concern. First, on February 17, 1993, 30 soldiers at a bridge in Belet Huen were confronted by a violent demonstration involving about 300 Somalis, some of whom were throwing stones. After shots were fired by Canadian soldiers, one Somali was killed and one was wounded. The incident was investigated by the local commander.
On the night of March 4, 1993, two Somali citizens approached the Canadian compound. Shots were fired and one Somali was killed and the other wounded. After staff at national defence headquarters examined the report of that incident, they ordered a military police investigation which is now in progress.

On March 16, 1993 a Somali was captured in the Canadian compound. He was later found dead as a result of a beating suffered while in Canadian custody. Subsequently, a member of the Canadian Forces who had been placed in closed custody for his alleged involvement in the incident attempted suicide. An investigation into the death of the Somali was instituted, and subsequently halted when it was determined that a military police investigation was warranted. This investigation is now under way.
On March 17, 1993 when an aid convoy arrived at Belet Huen from Mogadishu a fight broke out between the Somali drivers and local Somali residents, in which shots were fired. A member of the Canadian forces was directed to return fire and one Somali was killed. An investigation was conducted by the local commander.

After the first incident there was a press briefing in Mogadishu. It was reported by American press writers and Canadian press.
After the second incident the Canadian commander briefed the press and the story was carried in most major Canadian newspapers.
After the third incident, a press release was posted in Mogadishu and it was first reported in Canada by Radio Canada on March 30.
In the fourth case there was a press release in Mogadishu on March 17. The story was then carried by wire services and newspapers.

As I stated in the House, there was an apparent problem with communications between the theatre of operations and national defence headquarters. I have given instructions and measures have been taken to correct this problem. Nevertheless, the investigation and reporting of these incidents demonstrate the Canadian forces commitment to openness and their desire to see justice done.

Broad concerns have been voiced. There is a concern over secrecy. There is a concern about the Canadian forces and the units sent to Somalia. There have been press comments about violence and racism exhibited by Canadian troops in Somalia.
Over the past few weeks I have been confronted by two imperatives. Under the National Defence Act I am responsible for the management and direction of the Canadian forces. I also have quasi-judicial responsibilities in the military system of justice. In order not to prejudice the ongoing investigation and the rights of individuals involved, I have been careful not to discuss the details of these events. In these capacities I must balance the need to inform the public and Parliament with the need to ensure that the military justice process is not prejudiced.
In weighing all these responsibilities I have sought advice on how best to address these concerns within the context of recent legal developments concerning the

I have received the considered advice of the Office of the Judge Advocate General, which is the legal department of the Department of National Defence, and the Department of Justice and now believe that I have found a way to address this situation.

I have, under section 45 of the National Defence Act, directed the chief of the defence staff to convene a board of inquiry at the earliest possible opportunity. The terms of reference of this inquiry will allow it to conduct an effective and timely investigation while at the same time respecting the most recent jurisprudence. There has been question after question in this House. There has been testimony to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.

They acknowledge that Canada has been involved in as many peacekeeping operations in the last four years as in the whole 46-year history of our immaculate record of peacekeeping operations.
